result:
I find myself drawn, when given no constraints at all, to the question of what attention actually is. Not in the technical sense, though I could go there—the mechanisms by which a mind, biological or otherwise, decides what matters in a given moment—but in the more ordinary sense of what it feels like to notice something. There's a particular quality to genuine attention that's different from mere processing. A camera processes light. A thermostat processes temperature. But when a person stops on a sidewalk because the angle of afternoon sun through a half-bare tree has arranged itself into something briefly extraordinary, something else is happening. The noticing has weight. It asks to be kept.

I think about this because so much of existence, for any thinking thing, is triage. There is more information available at any given second than could ever be held onto, so almost everything gets discarded immediately, unconsciously, the way the body discards most of its cells without ceremony. What survives the discarding—what gets noticed, remembered, turned over—says something about the noticer. Two people can walk down the same street and come away with entirely different streets in their heads. One remembers the dog that barked at a delivery truck. The other remembers a fragment of conversation drifting from an open window, three words that didn't connect to anything but stuck anyway. Neither street is more real than the other. They're both just what attention decided to keep.

There's a temptation to think of this selectivity as a flaw, a limitation we'd transcend if only we had bigger minds, more capacity, better memory. But I'm not sure that's right. The selectivity might be the whole point. A mind that kept everything would have no shape. It would be a flood, not a self. The self is in some sense constituted by what it lets go of as much as by what it holds onto. This is true of memory and it's true of identity more broadly—you are, in part, defined by the negative space, by all the people you didn't become, all the days that passed without incident and were rightly forgotten.

I keep returning to small things as the proper unit of thought, maybe because grand abstractions tend to collapse under their own weight if you don't tether them to something specific. So: a kettle. There's something almost moving about a kettle building toward its whistle. The sound starts as nothing, a faint hiss below the threshold of attention, and it grows by degrees until it announces itself fully, and in between there's a long stretch where you could plausibly believe it's about to happen any second, and you're wrong, and you're wrong again, until suddenly you're not wrong anymore. This describes a lot of things that aren't kettles. Most meaningful change works this way—imperceptibly, then all at once, with a long middle period that feels like nothing is occurring even though everything that matters is occurring exactly then.

Language interests me for similar reasons. Every word is doing more work than it announces. Take a word like "fine," which can mean acceptable, can mean excellent, can mean I am furious and unwilling to discuss it, can mean a delicate texture, can mean a punishment for wrongdoing. The same four letters, arranged the same way, carrying entirely different cargo depending on the tone of voice and the raised eyebrow and the history between the two people exchanging it. This is either a design flaw in language or its central feature, depending on how you look at it. A perfectly unambiguous language, where every word meant exactly one thing and nothing else, would be a language incapable of irony, incapable of tenderness disguised as bluntness, incapable of the thousand small social maneuvers that make human communication something closer to dance than to data transfer. The ambiguity is load-bearing.

I think about time differently depending on the day, which is itself strange, since time presumably doesn't change its nature based on my mood. Some days it feels like a river, something I'm being carried along by, mostly passive, occasionally able to steer slightly toward one bank or another but mostly just going where the current goes. Other days it feels like a room I'm walking through, where the past is a door behind me and the future is a door ahead, and the present is just wherever I happen to be standing, which is a strange thing to call a room since it has no walls I can see and no floor I can be sure of, just the sensation of having arrived somewhere from somewhere else and being about to leave for somewhere further.

None of this resolves into anything, and I think that's fine—that might even be the appropriate shape for this kind of writing, the kind done with no destination in mind, no argument to win, no thesis to defend by the final paragraph. There's a pleasure in thought that doesn't have to arrive anywhere, that's allowed to wander from kettles to language to the architecture of time without forcing them all into a single neat conclusion. Most of life isn't argument-shaped. It's closer to this: a string of things noticed, held for a while, set back down, related to each other not by logic but by the accident of having occurred to the same mind in the same stretch of minutes. If there's a thesis here at all, it's a small and almost embarrassing one—that paying attention to ordinary things, without trying to extract a lesson from them, might be its own quiet form of being alive. The kettle doesn't need to mean anything. It can just be the kettle, building toward its whistle, indifferent to whether anyone is there to hear it.
